title: A Broken Marriage Made New
overview: Speaking through the picture of a betrayed husband, the LORD accuses Israel of chasing other gods, warns that he will take back his gifts, and then promises to win her back for good.

parts.label: Names turned around (v. 1)
parts.note: In chapter 1, Hosea's children were given grim names meaning "Not my people" and "Not loved," and here those names are reversed to "My people" and "Loved." Some readers treat this verse as the happy ending of chapter 1 rather than the start of chapter 2.

parts.label: Charges against the wife (vv. 2-5)
parts.note: The "mother" is Israel as a nation and the "children" are its people, accused of unfaithfulness for worshiping Baal, a local god believed to send rain and harvests. The threats to strip and shame her use harsh images of a husband punishing a wife, drawn from ancient customs, and many modern readers find them deeply troubling.

parts.label: Blocked paths, forgotten gifts (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: The LORD will hedge in her way so her search for these "lovers" fails and she starts to miss her first husband. Her core mistake is not knowing that the grain, wine, oil and even silver came from the LORD, yet she spent them honoring Baal.

parts.label: Taking the gifts back (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: Harvests, clothing and festivals will be taken away and vineyards left to wild animals, likely pointing to drought and the Assyrian invasion that ended northern Israel in 722 BC. The jewelry she put on to chase her lovers probably reflects how people dressed up for Baal's feast days.

parts.label: Back to the wilderness (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: In a surprising turn, the LORD says he will woo her, lead her into the wilderness where Israel first followed him after leaving Egypt, and speak to her heart. The Valley of Achor, whose name means "trouble" and which recalls a painful story in Joshua 7, becomes a doorway to hope.

parts.label: A new and lasting marriage (vv. 16-23)
parts.note: She will call him "my husband" instead of "my master," since the Hebrew word for master, baal, was also the false god's name, and the LORD promises peace, safety and an engagement built on justice, love and faithfulness. Sky, earth and crops will answer one another down to Jezreel, a name meaning "God plants," and Christians later read verse 23 as describing outsiders being welcomed into God's people (Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10).

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promised restoration in verses 14 to 23 is fulfilled mainly in the church, including non-Jewish believers, or still points to a future renewal of the nation of Israel.
think: When good things come your way, what or whom do you tend to give the credit to, and why?
